source.version: ASEE 2024 Annual Conference & Exposition proceedings paper, Paper ID #43798 (13-page PDF from peer.asee.org); all 13 PDF pages read
source.title_on_document: ChatGPT and Me: Collaborative Creativity in a Group Brainstorming with Generative AI

paper_design_summary: In a graduate product engineering course (spring 2023), 33 students were randomly assigned to 8 brainstorming groups of 3 to 5. Half of the groups (GA) could prompt ChatGPT inside their Microsoft Teams group chat and the other half (GB) could not; each group submitted 10 product ideas per week for two weeks. Combined groups of GA and GB students picked the top 5 ideas from the pooled 20, and the paper compares the share of picks from GA with 0.5 and compares TF-IDF cosine distances among groups' ideas within GA and within GB.

studies.label: Classroom group brainstorming with and without ChatGPT (two weeks)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly assigned to 8 brainstorming groups; ChatGPT access was then given to half of the groups (GA). The paper does not say how the groups that received ChatGPT were chosen.
assignment.quote: a cohort of 33 students was randomly assigned to 8 brainstorming groups, comprising 3 to 5 students per group. [...] In half of the groups (designated as GA), ChatGPT was introduced

arms.name: GA (ChatGPT)
arms.description: 4 groups that could prompt ChatGPT (user name iBot) directly in their Microsoft Teams group chat

arms.name: GB (no ChatGPT)
arms.description: 4 groups that brainstormed without ChatGPT; their chats were monitored to confirm ChatGPT was not used

participants.exclusions: None stated. Arm counts (17 GA, 16 GB) are the column sums of Table 2 (GA: 5, 3, 5, 4; GB: 4, 4, 4, 4; totals 9, 7, 9, 8 = 33). The paper prints no arm totals.
participants.who: Graduate students in a product engineering course at a large private university in the western United States, spring semester 2023
participants.quote: For a two-week time period, a cohort of 33 students was randomly assigned to 8 brainstorming groups, comprising 3 to 5 students per group.
participants.locator: p. 4, Education context & dataset description; p. 5, Table 2

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT (model version not stated), added to the group chat under the user name iBot
ai_tool.how_used: Students in GA prompted ChatGPT directly within their Microsoft Teams group chat, and the responses were posted in the same chat (p. 4, Figure 1).

task.description: Each group generated and submitted 10 product ideas per week for a user scenario on preventing COVID-19 (two similar scenarios, Table 1). At the end of each week, combined groups (Gcomb) of GA and GB students chose the top 5 most creative ideas from their pool of 20.

outcomes.name: Perceived creativity: share of top-5 ideas selected in combined groups that came from GA (RA)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Peer selection: each combined group (Gcomb, students from both arms) chose the 5 most creative ideas from the pooled 20 and attributed each to GA or GB; RA is the GA share, tested against 0.5. A linear regression of RA on week, group, and the GA student share found no significant effects (p = 0.444, 0.397, 0.411).

contrasts.reported: Wilcoxon signed-rank test that E[RA] != 0.5: p-value of 0.012; over the two weeks E[RA] is 0.725, i.e., on average 3.625 of the top-5 ideas selected in Gcomb came from GA

outcomes.name: Similarity of ideas across groups: pairwise cosine distance between groups' TF-IDF idea vectors
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Each group's 10 weekly ideas are combined into one TF-IDF vector (after SpaCy lemmatization and stopword removal); pairwise cosine distances among the 4 groups in each arm, per week. Higher distance means more diverse, so a smaller distance in GA would mean homogenization.

contrasts.reported: Pairwise distances within both GA and GB 'consistently fall within the range of 0.8 to 0.92 throughout both weeks'; t-tests show no significance (p values of 0.9624 and 0.3375 for weeks 1 and 2). Figure 6 cells: Week 1 GA 0.80, 0.82, 0.89, 0.81, 0.84, 0.86; GB 0.84, 0.83, 0.92, 0.91, 0.63, 0.90. Week 2 GA 0.67, 0.75, 0.75, 0.87, 0.86, 0.45; GB 0.81, 0.82, 0.83, 0.89, 0.58, 0.92.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance between TF-IDF vectors (range 0 to 1)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of groups within an arm, per week; each group's 10 ideas pooled into one TF-IDF vector (6 pairs per arm per week, per Figure 6)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: t-test comparing the distributions of pairwise distances in GA and GB, separately by week
diversity_detail.notes: The text's 0.8 to 0.92 range does not match several Figure 6 cells (0.45, 0.58, 0.63, 0.67, 0.75).

outcomes.name: Idea length (words per idea after pre-processing)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean word count per idea after SpaCy lemmatization and stopword removal. Related vocabulary measures: GA used 573 unique words vs 376 in GB over two weeks; Jensen-Shannon divergence between the arms' term-frequency distributions 0.4094 (p. 7, Figure 3).

contrasts.reported: Ideas generated with ChatGPT contain on average 14.92 words vs 10.5 words for student-generated ideas; 'statistically significant at the 0.001 level'

eligibility.reason: 33 students in total (Table 2: 17 in ChatGPT groups, 16 in no-ChatGPT groups), below 50. Students were randomly assigned to 8 groups, but the paper does not say how the 4 ChatGPT groups were chosen. Peer-selected creativity and TF-IDF diversity are scored on the ideas. Listed in the screening report as a small experiment.

one_line_finding: Ideas from ChatGPT groups made up 0.725 of peer-selected top-5 ideas (Wilcoxon test against 0.5, p = 0.012), and TF-IDF cosine distances among groups' ideas did not differ between arms (t-test p = 0.9624 week 1, 0.3375 week 2) (pp. 6 and 9).

applied.quote: For a two-week time period, a cohort of 33 students was randomly assigned to 8 brainstorming groups, comprising 3 to 5 students per group. [...] In half of the groups (designated as GA), ChatGPT was introduced
